text: If you can show it, don't say it.
Enter the scene as late as possible. Leave as early as you can.
A character is what they do under pressure, not what they say at peace.
Every scene must end on a different value charge than it started.
If your antagonist doesn't think they're the hero, you don't have one.
Don't confuse busy with active. A character can sit still and be more active than someone running.
The ending must be inevitable but not predictable.
Specific details are universal. Generalities are nobody's life.
Cut on motion. Cut on emotion. Never both.
Coverage isn't a safety net for indecision. Plan the cuts before you shoot.
When in doubt, hold longer. The audience will lean in.
Sound is half the film. Plan it before the shoot, not after.
A great film is made three times: in the script, on the set, and in the edit.
Every frame should answer: who is this scene about, and what do they want right now?
If the actor can play it without the line, cut the line.
Good direction looks like nothing. Bad direction looks like everything.
A subplot must deepen the theme or develop the protagonist. Otherwise it's filler.
If you can't pitch your film in one sentence, you don't yet know what it is.
Setup, then forget. Payoff lands hardest when the audience has stopped expecting it.
The protagonist must be the one who decides. If the world decides for them, they aren't the protagonist.
Casting against type forces an audience to look. Casting to type lets them stop looking.
Location is the third character. Pick it like one.
If your hero gets what they want at the end, you wrote a fairy tale. If they get what they need, you wrote drama.
Wide shots establish power. Close-ups establish vulnerability. Choose deliberately.
Great editing makes you feel like the cuts were inevitable. There were no other places.
A film is only as good as its midpoint twist.
Recce in the conditions you'll shoot in. Daytime recces of night shoots are theatre.
Rehearse blocking before lighting. Light the blocking, not the marks.
Constraints aren't restrictions. They're redistribution. What you save somewhere, you spend where it matters.
If the audience is asking "why is this scene here," the answer should be obvious one cut later.
A great score doesn't decorate the scene. It tightens it.
If you're cutting a scene you love because it doesn't serve the film, you're directing.
Trust the audience. They're smarter than your producer thinks.
First-time directors over-shoot. Second-time directors under-shoot. Third-time directors shoot exactly what they need.
If two characters agree on everything, you have one character.
Conflict is not argument. It's two needs that can't both be satisfied.
Your film's thesis is in its final image. Get the final image right.
A long take is not better than a cut. It's just different. Pick the one the scene needs.
If a flashback isn't carrying information the present can't, cut it.
Voiceover is a tool, not a crutch. Use it to add a layer, never to explain a scene.
Direction isn't moving the camera. It's deciding what the audience needs to feel right now.
If your DOP doesn't argue with you sometimes, you're not collaborating.
Pre-production is where you direct the film. The shoot is where you protect it.
An actor's worst take with intention is better than their best take without it.
If you're directing the actor's face instead of the actor's intent, you're micromanaging.
Shoot for the edit you want, not the edit your assistant editor will make easy.
A film's tone must be set in the first three minutes. The audience contracts with you there.
Don't fall in love with your draft. Fall in love with the film it could become.
The script is a blueprint, not a contract. Be loyal to the story, not the page.
Make the film you want to watch, not the film you think will sell. The first one might be both.
